solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rocket engine with discoloration in charger?

indicators.note: 'discoloration in charger' puts the stain inside the charger, as a mark sits in cloth

parts.note: a suer brings a charge against someone

explanation.surface: An electric car charger has gone a strange colour, as if blamed on a rocket motor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charger' looks like a battery charger or a warhorse; here it is one who charges in court, a SUER. The US spelling 'discoloration' is how the Times printed it.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical term: the second-stage motor that keeps a missile going after the booster burns out.

clue.text: Small instrument pitched too high

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A little instrument that plays out of tune, too high.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface keeps us in music throughout, so the definition hides in plain sight at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term: a note sung slightly above its true pitch is said to be sharp, the opposite of flat.

clue.text: Outside water sports champion?

parts.note: to surf is a water sport

explanation.surface: Someone who is a champion at outdoor water sports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' reads as an adjective on 'water sports', but it is the noun definition standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the outermost layer or face of any object, the noun sense of 'Outside'.

clue.text: Western missing out on Oscar after head of Academy noted exception

indicators.note: the shortened word is placed after that letter
only the first letter of the next word
a letter is left out, as if the word missed it

parts.note: O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Western film fails to win an Oscar, which the Academy head calls an exception.
explanation.walkthrough: The Academy and Oscar suggest the film awards, but they just supply letters. 'Noted' makes the definition musical.
explanation.definitionFit: In music an accidental is a sharp, flat or natural sign outside the key signature, an exception on the stave.

clue.text: Out to lunch in New York eating sandwich with no crust

indicators.note: the outer letters take in, as if eating, the trimmed word
the outside letters are cut away, like crusts off bread

parts.note: a butty is British slang for a sandwich

explanation.surface: Someone out at lunch in New York, eating a crustless sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out to lunch' looks like literal lunchtime, but it is the idiom for being crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Out to lunch is an informal idiom for crazy or eccentric, just as nutty is.

clue.text: Returning from break in the middle of jury service

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it into pieces, which are then reassembled in a new order
the middle of a word is its central letters, here the two at the heart of jury

parts.note: the two central letters of jURy

explanation.surface: Coming back from a break partway through doing jury service.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a juror back from lunch; 'break' is the anagram instruction, and only the middle of 'jury' joins the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A mathematical sense: a process that calls or loops back on itself keeps returning to its own start.

clue.text: Nark's pressing question into the scoring of more ecstasy

indicators.note: to press one thing into another is to push it inside

parts.note: più is Italian for 'more', as written in a musical score (più forte)

explanation.surface: An informer pushing questions about scoring more ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nark' reads as a police informer in a drugs story; it is the verb meaning irritate. 'Scoring' means written in a musical score, not buying drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A British colloquial verb: to nark someone is to irritate them, to wound their pride.

clue.text: Hide large treasure boxes

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it

parts.note: a treasure, a darling, is a pet

explanation.surface: Hide the big treasure chests away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' and 'boxes' read as hiding treasure in chests; 'Hide' is the noun, an animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: an animal's skin with the fur or hair still on.

clue.text: Parquet floor's finish getting damaged on shifting piano a fraction

indicators.note: getting damaged letters are knocked about, so they are rearranged
the piano is shifted out, removed from the pool of letters
the final letter of the word before

parts.note: the word floor, in its possessive form
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A parquet floor gets scratched when the piano is moved across it.
explanation.walkthrough: PARQUET plus R, the end of 'floor', rearranged ('damaged') with P taken out ('shifting piano').
explanation.definitionFit: A quarter is one of four equal parts, a common fraction.

clue.text: Conclude ultimately that women supply dowry?

indicators.note: read as 'supplely', flexibly: the letters bend into a new order
ultimately means in the end, so we take the letter at the very end of 'that'

explanation.surface: A conclusion that it is women who must provide the dowry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a verb with women as its subject; it is the adverb of supple, loosening T and WOMEN into OWMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a dowry is property settled on a marriage, one kind of gift that endows.

clue.text: Fruit and a lot of cereal in a jar

indicators.note: the shortened cereal goes inside the jar
a lot of the word, not all of it: the last letter goes

explanation.surface: Someone stores fruit along with plenty of cereal in a jar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' leaves the cereal one letter short, and 'in a jar' places it inside the pot after the opening 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit related to the peach and plum.

clue.text: Greens arrested without a shred of evidence

indicators.note: the letter is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: to be collared is to be arrested

indicators.note: just one tiny bit, the opening letter, of the next word

explanation.surface: Environmental protesters taken into custody with no evidence against them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greens' suggests eco-campaigners, but here it means leafy vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Collard is a cabbage-family plant whose leaves are eaten as greens, especially in the American South.

clue.text: Tartan Army held back by copper dispersing a party in Cardiff

parts.note: a plaid is a tartan cloth

indicators.note: the reversed letters are held inside the metal's symbol
the holding is done by the copper symbol

parts.note: CU is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: the letters are read backwards
the letter is dispersed, sent away from the word

explanation.surface: Scotland football fans, the Tartan Army, held up by a policeman while a party goes on in Cardiff.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tartan Army is the nickname of Scotland's football supporters, and a copper is a policeman; both are misdirection. 'Held back by' splits: 'back' reverses, 'held by' contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid Cymru is the Welsh nationalist political party, and Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

clue.text: Store Tesco's opening in Berkshire perhaps

indicators.note: the opening of anything is its start, so the first letter of Tesco

parts.note: the Berkshire is a breed of pig, and a sow is a female pig

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

explanation.surface: A Tesco supermarket store opening somewhere in the county of Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times first printed STEW, an error it later corrected to STOW. Tesco is a British supermarket chain, and Berkshire looks like the English county but is the pig breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to put things away for keeping.

clue.text: Priest's backing change and still preaching about it

indicators.note: a preacher speaks, so the words are heard aloud rather than read

parts.note: to alter is to change, and peace is stillness, giving alter peace

explanation.surface: A priest backs change while staying calm in sermons about it.
explanation.walkthrough: ALTER and PEACE, said aloud, sound like the answer; the definition reads 'backing' as what stands behind the priest.
explanation.definitionFit: An altarpiece is a painting or carving set behind the altar, so it forms the backdrop where the priest officiates.

clue.text: Affected by a tinge of nostalgia in middle of poem

indicators.note: a tinge is only a trace of colour, so only a trace of the word, its first letter

explanation.surface: A poem whose central stanza is tinged with nostalgia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In middle of' looks like a place in the poem; with 'poem' it is the definition, the poetic clipped form of between.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic form: the clipped 'between' of verse means in the middle of.

clue.text: Cut up leaf to brew this amount?

definitions.text: Cut up leaf to brew this amount?

indicators.note: brewing stirs and steeps the leaves, and it stirs the letters too

explanation.surface: Chop tea leaves to make a certain quantity of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: cut-up leaf is what you brew into a cup's worth.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: chopped tea leaf, brewed, gives one cup's measure.

clue.text: Very obvious line penned by gag writer with only one good set

indicators.note: the letter is enclosed, as in a pen, by the jumbled letters
set in the sense of arranged, so the letters are rearranged
one of the two matching letters is dropped

explanation.surface: A comedy writer with a single good joke routine slips in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a comedy set, but it is the anagram signal, as in set out in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Writ large is an idiom meaning shown clearly or on a grand scale, so plain to see.

clue.text: Alert wife understanding waves from pram?

parts.note: an idea of something is an understanding of it
a pram is a small flat-bottomed boat, and its wake is the waves it leaves

explanation.surface: An attentive wife noticing a baby waving from its pram.
explanation.walkthrough: The pram is a baby's carriage in the surface and a small boat in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: fully awake, with eyes wide open, and so on the alert.

clue.text: Exhausted trooper in a seat like this?

indicators.note: something exhausted has been emptied, so only the outer letters of trooper remain

explanation.surface: A worn-out cavalry trooper slumped in the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'like this' points back at the picture: a trooper in a saddle sits with a leg on each side.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a rider in a saddle sits with a leg on either side, the posture the clue pictures.

clue.text: Fit cap of tiny brown liquor bottle

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it up inside
the cap is the top of anything, so in a down answer the first letter

explanation.surface: Put the cap back on a little bottle of brown liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like a verb about putting on a cap; it is the noun, an outburst.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: a sudden outburst of bad temper, especially a child's.

clue.text: Charlie wearing a lush cravat

indicators.note: someone wearing a garment has it wrapped round them

parts.note: a lush is a drunkard, a sot
C = Charlie in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie, dressed in a luxurious neck-tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' reads as the adjective, luxurious; it is the noun, a drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: this broad neck scarf takes its name from Royal Ascot, where it was fashionable racewear.

clue.text: Wild cat — he twice spotted one in the Serengeti

indicators.note: wild letters run free, so they are rearranged
the word he is put into the pool two times over

explanation.surface: A safari-goer sees a wild cat with spots, mentioned in the Serengeti.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' looks like part of the definition, but it rearranges CAT plus HE twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is a spotted big cat of the African savannah, common on Tanzania's plains.

clue.text: Brief exercise involving Navy vessels

indicators.note: 'Brief' cuts a letter off

explanation.surface: A short naval exercise with the fleet's ships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels' in a navy story wants to be ships; here they are pots.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: large vases for ashes or tea are vessels in the container sense.

clue.text: Scottish writer's terror on hearing what lies deep below

indicators.note: on hearing it, the phrase is listened to rather than spelt

parts.note: J. M. Barrie, author of Peter Pan, was a Scottish writer, and terror is fear, giving Barrie's fear

explanation.surface: A Scottish author's fear is revealed when hearing what lurks far underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: BARRIE'S FEAR, said aloud, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The barysphere is the dense interior of the Earth beneath the crust, the planet's deep core region.

clue.text: Check on board capsized river boat

indicators.note: cargo on board a ship sits inside it
a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down answer the river is written bottom to top

parts.note: the Tay is a Scottish river

explanation.surface: Checking on board a boat that capsized on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check on board' reads as an inspection; it is chess, CH, going aboard the upturned river.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sailing or motor vessel built for pleasure is one kind of boat.

clue.text: Soreness when pulling off a river wader

indicators.note: to pull something off is to remove it, so the R is taken away

parts.note: soreness in the sense of rueful regret

explanation.surface: Someone's legs aching after hauling a wader off by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests fishing waders; the wader is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this white heron is one of the birds that wade in shallow water.

clue.text: Tip a fraction of a pound following our short drink

indicators.note: the tipped piece comes after the shortened one
the word is cut short, losing its last letter
to tip something is to turn it over, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: an ounce, OZ, is one sixteenth of a pound

explanation.surface: Instructions for a barman: tip in a small measure after our quick drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Ouzo is an anise-flavoured Greek spirit, a strong alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Steps required for returning chimney in Glasgow area

indicators.note: to return is to come back

explanation.surface: Stairs needed to reach a chimney somewhere in Glasgow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steps' reads as stairs up to the chimney; it is a procedure, and 'for' is part of the wordplay, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fixed method or recipe is the set of steps needed to get a result.

clue.text: Maker of all my sandwiches put away on launch of restaurant

indicators.note: the bread of a sandwich lies either side of the filling

parts.note: 'Cor!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise

indicators.note: 'on' in the sense of added after
the launch of anything is its start, so the first letter of restaurant

parts.note: to put away food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone who made all my sandwiches, eaten when a restaurant opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maker of all my sandwiches' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'all': God.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet of God: the Nicene Creed calls him 'maker of heaven and earth, of all things'.

clue.text: Bachelor parking large car outside dance

parts.note: a limo, a limousine, is a large car

explanation.surface: A bachelor parking a stretch limo outside a dance hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a stag night; the dance is the one done under a low bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the West Indian dance done by bending backwards under a lowered bar.

clue.text: Pedal spring obtained from cycling centre to the west of Derby?

indicators.note: in an across answer west is left, so this piece comes first
the first letter of the word cycles round to the end

parts.note: a derby is a bowler hat

explanation.surface: Pedalling on a bike from the town centre westward toward Derby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' and 'Pedal' suggest bikes and 'Derby' an English city, but Derby is the American name for a bowler hat.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrechat is a ballet leap where the dancer crosses the feet in the air, a spring done with the feet.
